docs.title: Obsidian Sync Server
docs.text:
A headless sync hub running as a Docker container that integrates:

  • 💎 Obsidian Sync (official obsidian-headless client)
  • ☁️ Nextcloud Sync (nextcloudcmd client)
  • 📝 Google Keep (pulling notes via gkeepapi)

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text:
The server acts as a central hub (the "Local Vault") mediating data flow between three separate platforms.

graph TD
    Keep[📝 Google Keep] -->|Periodic Pull| Vault[(📂 Local Vault)]
    Vault <-->|Continuous| Obs[💎 Obsidian Sync Server]
    Vault <-->|Periodic| NC[☁️ Nextcloud Server]

docs.title: 📝 Google Keep Integration
docs.text:
• One-way Pull: Imports notes matching required tags as Markdown files into a designated vault folder.
  • Advanced Tag Extraction & AI Integration: Extracts inline hashtags and Labels: lines directly from the Keep note body. This is especially powerful for notes saved via AI assistants like Google Gemini. While Gemini cannot natively apply Keep labels, it automatically attaches a URL annotation to the note. You can prompt Gemini to include text tags (e.g., #idea) in the note body. The syncer uses the annotation to identify these notes, extracts your inline tags, writes them back to the Google Keep note as native labels, and includes them in your Obsidian Markdown frontmatter.
  • Smart Tag Matching: Case-insensitive matching of required, ignored, and extracted tags.
  • Sync State Tracking: Optionally applies a configured label (e.g., synced) to the original Keep note to prevent re-importing the same note twice.
  • Flexible Authentication: Supports standard Google credentials and master token flow.

docs.title: ☁️ Nextcloud Synchronization
docs.text:
• Bidirectional Sync: Periodically synchronizes your local vault with your Nextcloud instance.
  • Conflict Management: Automatically prioritizes Obsidian as the source of truth, cleaning up Nextcloud conflict files (_conflict-*) to prevent sync loops.

docs.title: 💎 Obsidian Sync Integration
docs.text:
• Real-time Sync: Runs the official obsidian-headless client continuously to ensure near-instant sync with your other devices.
  • Process Management: Monitors and automatically restarts the background client if it crashes.

docs.title: The Sync Process
docs.text:
The server runs in daemon mode and orchestrates synchronization tasks for each of your configured "sync sets" (vaults).

Continuous Sync:

  • Obsidian Sync: The official obsidian-headless client is launched as a persistent background process. It runs continuously, observing your vault directory and pushing/pulling changes in real-time with the Obsidian Sync servers.

Periodic Sync (Every 5 minutes by default):

Every sync interval, the main Python daemon wakes up and performs the following sequence for each vault:

  1. Keep Alive: It verifies the Obsidian Sync background process is still running and healthy, restarting it if necessary.
  2. Google Keep Pull: It connects to Google Keep via gkeepapi. It searches for active notes matching your configured tags (while ignoring any ignore_tags). It converts matching notes to Markdown, enriches them with frontmatter, and saves them into the designated target_folder. Finally, it applies the mark_synced_tag to the Keep note.
  3. Nextcloud Sync: It invokes nextcloudcmd to synchronize your local vault directory with your remote Nextcloud server. This ensures all your Obsidian notes (and your newly imported Keep notes) are backed up to Nextcloud.

Conflict Resolution

In this architecture, Obsidian is considered the authoritative source of truth. To prevent sync loops and duplicate files, any conflict files generated by Nextcloud (_conflict-*) are automatically deleted during the Nextcloud sync phase. Obsidian's own conflict resolution strategy will handle any underlying discrepancies.

docs.title: Sync Cycle Sequence
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the exact ordering of operations within a single periodic sync cycle, and how it interacts with the continuously running Obsidian Sync process.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Daemon as Python Daemon
    participant OB as Obsidian Sync (background)
    participant FS as Local Vault (filesystem)
    participant GK as Google Keep API
    participant NC as Nextcloud Server

    Note over OB,FS: Obsidian Sync runs continuously,<br/>watching the vault directory

    loop Every 5 minutes
        Daemon->>OB: Health check (restart if crashed)

        rect rgb(60, 60, 90)
            Note over Daemon,GK: Phase 1 — Google Keep Pull
            Daemon->>GK: Authenticate (with retry)
            GK-->>Daemon: Session
            Daemon->>GK: Fetch all notes
            GK-->>Daemon: Notes list
            Daemon->>Daemon: Filter by tags, extract inline tags
            Daemon->>FS: Atomic write (.tmp → rename)
            Daemon->>GK: Add synced tag to note
            Daemon->>GK: Push label changes (with retry)
        end

        rect rgb(60, 90, 60)
            Note over Daemon,NC: Phase 2 — Nextcloud Sync
            Daemon->>NC: nextcloudcmd (with retry, creds via env)
            NC-->>FS: Bidirectional sync
            Daemon->>FS: Delete conflict files (log content first)
        end

        Daemon->>FS: Write healthcheck timestamp

        Note over OB,FS: Obsidian Sync picks up<br/>new/changed files automatically
    end

docs.title: One-Way Archive Semantics (Google Keep)
docs.text: The sync from Google Keep is strictly one-way pull. Deleting a note in Google Keep does not delete the corresponding file from the local vault. Your vault acts as a permanent archive of imported notes. This is intentional — once a note is in your vault, it is yours to keep, reorganize, or delete manually.

docs.title: Obsidian as Source of Truth
docs.text: When conflicts arise between Obsidian Sync and Nextcloud, Obsidian wins. Nextcloud conflict files (*_conflict-*) are automatically deleted. Before deletion, the syncer logs a preview of the conflicting content so that data is not silently lost.

docs.title: Atomic File Writes
docs.text: When saving a Google Keep note to disk, the syncer writes to a temporary file (.tmp) and then atomically renames it to the final path. This prevents Obsidian Sync or Nextcloud from reading a half-written file.

docs.title: Crash Recovery
docs.text:
The mark_synced_tag is applied to a Keep note after the file is written but before it is pushed back to Keep. If the process crashes between writing the file and pushing the tag:

  • Worst case: the note is imported again on the next cycle, overwriting the existing file with identical content.
  • No data loss occurs because the file was already written atomically.

If the process crashes after pushing the tag but before Nextcloud sync, the file will simply be picked up by Nextcloud on the next cycle.

docs.title: Retry Strategy
docs.text: Network operations (Keep authentication, Keep sync push, Nextcloud sync) use exponential back-off with up to 3 retry attempts. Only transient errors (network timeouts, connection errors) are retried. Permanent errors (bad credentials) fail immediately.

docs.title: Container Health Monitoring
docs.text: The daemon writes a timestamp to /tmp/last_sync after each successful sync cycle. The Docker HEALTHCHECK verifies this timestamp is less than 10 minutes old. If three consecutive checks fail, Docker marks the container as unhealthy, which is visible via docker compose ps and can trigger restart policies.

docs.title: Google Keep
docs.text: To securely authenticate with Google Keep via gkeepapi, standard passwords and App Passwords are no longer supported for continuous syncing. Google's automated security blocks frequent login requests, so you MUST use a Master Token.

docs.title: Generating a Master Token
docs.text:
Run the included helper script to generate a Master Token:

uv run scripts/get_keep_token.py

The script supports two authentication flows. You can choose the one that works best for you.

Method 1: App Password Flow (Recommended) 1. Ensure you have 2-Step Verification enabled on your Google Account. 2. Navigate to Security and search for "App passwords". 3. Create a new App Password (e.g., for "Obsidian Syncer") and copy the 16-character string. 4. Run the script, select choice 1, and provide your email and the App Password.

Method 2: OAuth Cookie Flow (Alternative) If the App Password flow fails with a BadAuthentication error (often because Google temporarily blocks the request), use this alternative flow. 1. Open an incognito/private browser window. 2. Log into your Google account. 3. Navigate to https://accounts.google.com/EmbeddedSetup. 4. Open Developer Tools (F12) -> Application/Storage tab -> Cookies. 5. Find the cookie named oauth_token (starts with oauth2_4/) and copy its value. 6. Run the script, select choice 2, and provide your email and the copied cookie.

Final Step: The script will output a Master Token (starts with aas_et/). Use this Master Token as your KEEP_PASSWORD environment variable. Keep it secret!

Nextcloud Credentials

Pass your Nextcloud credentials via environment variables (NC_USER and NC_PASSWORD). The configuration file will dynamically expand these variables to prevent hardcoding secrets.

docs.title: Obsidian Headless
docs.text:
The obsidian-headless tool requires an active Obsidian Sync subscription. To authenticate, you should run the container interactively once:

  1. Open a terminal in the container: docker exec -it obsidian-syncer bash
  2. Run ob login and follow the prompts.
  3. Link the vault with ob sync-setup --vault "YourRemoteVaultName" --path /vaults/my_vault.
  4. Restart the container so the Python daemon picks up the new sync process.

docs.title: Setup Configuration
docs.text:
Create a config.yaml file mapping your sets:

config.yaml
sync_sets:
  - name: "my_vault"
    local_dir: "/vaults/my_vault"
    obsidian:
      enabled: true
    nextcloud:
      enabled: true
      url: "https://nextcloud.example.com"
      user: "${NC_USER}"
      password: "${NC_PASSWORD}"
      remote_folder: "/Obsidian/my_vault"
    keep:
      enabled: true
      username: "${KEEP_USER}"
      password: "${KEEP_PASSWORD}" # Use an App Password or Master Token
      tags: ["Obsidian"] # Note must have this tag (or have it extracted via inline_tags_label)
      include_filter_tags: false # Optional: Set to false to exclude 'tags' from frontmatter
      extra_tags: ["Imported"] # Optional: Extra tags to append to the Markdown frontmatter
      inline_tags_label: "Gemini" # Extract #tags from text for notes with this Keep label
      ignore_tags: ["synced"] # Notes with this tag will be skipped
      mark_synced_tag: "synced" # Auto-add this tag to a note after downloading it
      target_folder: "/vaults/my_vault/KeepNotes"

docs.title: Google Keep Syncing Options
docs.text:
• tags: A list of tags. The syncer will only pull notes from Google Keep that contain ALL of these tags.
  • include_filter_tags: (Optional) Boolean (default true). If set to false, the tags specified in tags will not be included in the rendered Markdown note's frontmatter.
  • extra_tags: (Optional) A list of tags to automatically include in the generated Obsidian frontmatter.
  • inline_tags_label: (Optional) A specific Keep label (e.g., "Gemini"). If a note has this label in Keep, the syncer will check the note's content for hashtags (e.g., #Obsidian #Idea) or a line starting with Labels: (e.g., Labels: tag1, tag2). These extracted tags are combined with the note's Keep labels and then checked against tags and ignore_tags. This is especially useful for notes created by external apps (like Gemini or Google Assistant) that cannot natively assign multiple Keep labels. Extracted tags are automatically written back to Google Keep as actual labels on the note, and are also added to the generated Obsidian frontmatter.
  • ignore_tags: (Optional) A list of tags. The syncer will skip any note that has ANY of these tags.
  • mark_synced_tag: (Optional) A single tag. The syncer will automatically add this tag to a note in Google Keep after it has successfully downloaded it. This is typically used in combination with ignore_tags to prevent a note from being downloaded again in the future.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Choose your preferred method to run the sync server:

Docker ComposeDocker CLI

For a more persistent setup, use Docker Compose. Create a docker-compose.yml:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  obsidian-syncer:
    image: ghcr.io/janlo/obsidian-syncer:latest
    container_name: obsidian-syncer
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./config.yaml:/config.yaml:ro
      - ./vaults:/vaults
      - ./ob-config:/root/.config
    environment:
      - NC_USER=${NC_USER}
      - NC_PASSWORD=${NC_PASSWORD}
      - KEEP_USER=${KEEP_USER}
      - KEEP_PASSWORD=${KEEP_PASSWORD}

Run it in the background: 

docker compose up -d

Run the container using a bind mount for the configuration, vaults, and obsidian configuration directory:

docker run -d \
  --name obsidian-syncer \
  -v $(pwd)/config.yaml:/config.yaml \
  -v $(pwd)/vaults:/vaults \
  -v $(pwd)/ob-config:/root/.config \
  -e NC_USER=... \
  -e NC_PASSWORD=... \
  -e KEEP_USER=... \
  -e KEEP_PASSWORD=... \
  ghcr.io/janlo/obsidian-syncer:latest

docs.title: Understanding the Volumes
docs.text: It might seem disconnected at first glance to have a single config.yaml file alongside mounted directories. This separation is a common Docker pattern that cleanly divides instructions from data and state:

docs.title: 1. config.yaml (The Instructions)
docs.text:
This file tells the daemon what to do (e.g., which sync sets to run, which tags to look for, and remote URLs). It is mounted as a read-only (:ro) file: 

- ./config.yaml:/config.yaml:ro
If you want to change your sync logic, you simply edit this file on your host machine.

docs.title: 2. ./vaults (Your Data Workspace)
docs.text:
This is where your actual Markdown .md files live. The config.yaml references this directory (e.g., local_dir: "/vaults/my_vault"). 

- ./vaults:/vaults
The container needs read and write access to pull and push files here. Mounting it ensures your notes are safely stored on your host machine and aren't lost when the container is recreated.

docs.title: 3. ./ob-config (The Memory & Internal State)
docs.text:
This directory is essential for authentication and caching. 

- ./ob-config:/root/.config
Tools like the ob CLI and nextcloudcmd store their session tokens and sync caches in the user's home directory. Without this mount, the container would have "amnesia" upon restarting, and you would lose your Obsidian Sync login session. Mounting it ensures your authentication state persists.

[!NOTE] In summary: The container boots up, reads your Instructions (config.yaml), uses its Memory (/root/.config) to remember you're already logged in, and manages your notes in the Workspace (/vaults).

docs.title: Health Monitoring
docs.text:
The Docker image includes a built-in HEALTHCHECK. After each successful sync cycle, the daemon writes a timestamp to an internal file. Docker verifies every 5 minutes that this timestamp is less than 10 minutes old.

You can check the container's health status at any time:

docker inspect --format='{{.State.Health.Status}}' obsidian-syncer

Or see it in the docker compose ps output:

docker compose ps
Status Meaning healthy The sync loop completed within the last 10 minutes. unhealthy The sync loop has not completed recently — check logs. starting The container just started and hasn't completed its first cycle yet.

Auto-Restart on Unhealthy

Docker Compose does not natively restart on unhealthy status, but you can add the autoheal container alongside your stack, or use Docker Swarm which supports restart_policy with health checks.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If you encounter issues during synchronization, you can enable more detailed logging by setting the LOG_LEVEL environment variable to DEBUG.

In your docker-compose.yml, add it to the environment section:

    environment:
      - LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG
      # ... other environment variables ...

Or pass it via the Docker CLI:

docker run -d \
  # ... other flags ...
  -e LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG \
  ghcr.io/janlo/obsidian-syncer:latest
